Your Private Practice Planner

What your caseload earns, what it costs, and how many reduced-fee slots you can carry.

Getting started

  1. Open Private-Practice-Planner.xlsx in Microsoft Excel on a desktop computer.
  2. If Excel opens it in Protected View, choose Enable Editing so the calculations run.
  3. Save your own copy and work in that.
  4. On Practice, set your weeks worked, your target take-home, and your own tax set-aside rate.
  5. Fill in one row per fee tier: what you charge, how many slots a week, and how often those slots are actually kept.
Attendance is the number most people guess. If you have a year of history, count the sessions that happened and divide by the slots you held. A guess works to start with, but the results are only as honest as this figure.

The four tabs

  • Practice — weeks, target, tax set-aside, and your fee tiers.
  • Costs — what you pay monthly and annually to keep the practice open.
  • Results — take-home, what the target needs, and your reduced-fee capacity.
  • Reference — every term, every assumption, and where to change it.

Before you start

A slot and a session are not the same thing. A slot is a place on your calendar. A session is one that happened. At 90% attendance a $150 slot is worth $135, and every figure that matters follows from that difference.
Reduced-fee capacity is a number, not a feeling. Enter your full fee, the reduced fee you want to offer, and your weekly slots. The sheet works out how many of those slots can be at the reduced fee while your target is still reached — and tells you when the answer is none.
This is arithmetic, not advice. It does not recommend a fee, a tax rate, a caseload, or a sliding-scale policy, and it contains nothing clinical. The tax set-aside is a rate you choose. Check it with your accountant.

Cell colors

  • Cream cells — enter your own numbers here.
  • Gray cells — calculated automatically. Do not type in these.
  • Blue cells — editable assumptions.
